text:
Yes. A commit's hash covers its parent, tree, author/committer metadata, and message. Rebase replays commits onto a new base, so each replayed commit gets a new parent (and usually a new committer timestamp), producing a new hash.

Exceptions: commits that end up with an identical parent, tree, and metadata keep their hashes. For example, commits below the point where the rebase starts are untouched, and a rebase that is a no-op (already based on the target) leaves everything as is. Also, `git rebase` fast-forwards when it can, reusing the original commits.

Because the hashes change, rebasing commits that others have already pulled forces them to reconcile diverged history, so avoid rebasing shared branches.
